Most people see $38B+ in volume and assume Jumper is printing money.

I ran the math and it's a different story.

The volume is real. 30M+ transactions, and the last 30 days alone were about $808M in bridge volume and $159M in swaps, with bridging up around 34% from the month before.

But on a $1,000 trade, Jumper makes anywhere from $0 to just $0.50, depending on what you're swapping. The fees look like this:

Stable swaps: 0%
Major swaps: 0.02%
Other swaps: 0.05%
Bridging is similarly cheap at roughly 0.01–0.05%.

I did some back-of-the-napkin math on what that adds up to. At those rates, last month's volume works out to somewhere around $80k to $480k in fees, so call it roughly $1M to $6M a year depending on the mix.

Which makes the upcoming $JUMP launch more interesting to me as a business-model test than as another token sale.

The distribution is clearly there, but turning all that activity into real money is the harder part.

I think that's exactly why Jumper is pushing beyond simple bridging into Earn, RWAs, advanced trading and perps. More products means more chances to actually monetize the users it already has.

It's also why I wouldn't obsess over the $75M sale FDV alone yet. The tokenomics are more interesting to me right now:

- 33.33% community
- 26.07% investors
- 14.7% team
- 21.9% treasury
- 4% public sale

Investor and team unlocks are delayed, but we still don't know how much of that 33.33% community slice is tradeable on day one, and that's gonna decide the opening float more than anything else here.

So what I'm watching is pretty simple:

1. How much of the community allocation unlocks at launch

2. Monthly fee revenue, and whether it moves off that $1M to $6M range

3. Any announcement tying the token to fees, whether buybacks, revenue share, or anything else

I'm probably off on some of the math, but I'd want answers to the last two before caring much about the FDV either way.

Anyways not a recommendation to buy in anyway, wanted to share some research we did.

I often get asked what skills we'll need to be “successful” in an AI future. After OpenAI DevDay, and using more bots, I'm adding executive function to the list.

1. Creativity, vision
2. Executive function (plan, focus, juggle multiple tasks) to manage bots
3. Empathy, community 

What will be less valuable is mastering a traditional skill, whether it’s accounting, software development, research, or, yes, asset management.

The bots are everywhere: OpenAI Dots, Muse, Siri, Grok Bot, Poke, Instinct, Gemini Spark, and they’re only going to get better.

This is a bigger week than most investors realize for $SPCX and they’re just scratching the surface.

Monday: Starship’s first orbital mission deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

Thursday: Three launches. First, a Falcon 9 launch from Florida with four crew members going to the International Space Station. Second, Falcon 9 will launch from California with 103 payloads. Third, Falcon Heavy will launch NROL-97, a U.S. spy satellite, from Florida (a different pad than the one earlier in the day).

Long-Term Launch Targets: This year, SpaceX will do about 170-180 missions. In August, Musk said that by 2030, the goal is 30 Starship launches a day. If they run Mon-Fri, that’s 6k a year. In other words, we’re 3% of the way there.

The Key Question: What is the real launch number in 2030? I believe a more likely number is 2,200 by 2030, which implies about doubling every year. This is a bigger week than most investors realize for $SPCX and they’re just scratching the surface.

Monday: Starship’s first orbital mission deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

Thursday: Three launches. First, a Falcon 9 launch from Florida with four crew members going to the International Space Station. Second, Falcon 9 will launch from California with 103 payloads. Third, Falcon Heavy will launch NROL-97, a U.S. spy satellite, from Florida (a different pad than the one earlier in the day).

Long-Term Launch Targets: This year, SpaceX will do about 170-180 missions. In August, Musk said that by 2030, the goal is 30 Starship launches a day. If they run Mon-Fri, that’s 6k a year. In other words, we’re 3% of the way there.

The Key Question: What is the real launch number in 2030? I believe a more likely number is 2,200 by 2030, which implies about doubling every year. If they get to that 2k-plus number, my guess is the stock more than doubles from here. A double would imply an average annual return of 30% during those four years.

tweets.text:
TLDR: like all markets crypto is becoming K-shaped in itself. you have two ends of th K - top end is growing fundamentals in growing businesses which will slowly accrue more flows over time

bottom K is on-chain getting rekt by lemon markets (read: Claude / AI making it incredibly difficult to differentiate real projects) - last time maybe you had 10 out of 100 projects that were good. now it's 10 out of 10,000. the % chance of getting needle in the haystack is lower and lower, and all value in the bottom of K will accrue to scammers, KOLs, or P&Ders

i wrote yesterday that catalyst trades don't work anymore for the same reason. in a K-shaped world, most of the money flows towards assets people are comfortable buying and holding in - taking one-off catalyst trades for protocols which otherwise have no underlying fundamentals is akin to playing at the poker table with a bunch of other starving people who have been rummaging through the trash (on-chain) and are desperate for some win. very simply, the flows don't support this anymore - and we've seen it in PA. sharp price action both ways.

and this is a feedback loop in and of itself. as more and more people lose money trying to play negative sum games (and these ARE negative sum games because everyone loses except the house), more and more people will flock to positive sum games (growing fundamentals are net winning for everyone, see HYPE as the best example) 

we've already seen this play out years and years in crypto. we are just finally at the culmination of it all. 2018, 2021, 2024, all the same shit. just that the only difference now is that you can opt out to play positive sum games, whereas in the past, you had no other choice. 

long those growing fundamentals. don't give a shit about the rest. and hold. 

i will say that the investors playbook is extremely clear right now, but majority of retail will still choose to play negative sum games either because they have deluded themselves into believing they have some sort of edge (1 big win => i am good => many small losses => lose it all) or they are too short term to do any of the stated above

it's really up to you. good luck.
